findings: scFed runs four classifiers (linear SVM, ACTINN fully connected network, XGBoost, Geneformer fine-tuning) in a simulated federation on eight public scRNA-seq datasets. Federated models match centralized ones on cell-type F1 (Wilcoxon, no significant difference) and beat local-only models except on the smallest dataset (Xin); F1 falls when clients rise from 10 to 20. Across datasets (leave-one-human-pancreas-dataset-out, three clients) the federated model again matched centralized and beat local. Prior-art relevance (Q6): it is federated classification of cells from expression only; the introduction names PriCell, scPrivacy and PPML-Omics as earlier federated single-cell work, and nothing in it concerns histology or prediction of expression from images. Heterogeneity (Q4): the only non-IID tests are pooling of different pancreas protocols and a two-sample COVID PBMC appendix, where giving each client a different patient lowered ACTINN/XGBoost/Geneformer federated F1.

caveats: Simulated federation on one machine with random or dataset-wise splits; clients are evenly sized random shards in the intra-dataset test, so label and feature heterogeneity is mild. Cell-type classification, not regression of expression. No privacy attack or differential privacy is run; the Discussion says shared updates can leak and proposes trusted execution or secure multi-party computation as future work. No personalisation or gene-panel mismatch is tested. Wilcoxon tests rest on five repetitions. Authors include an industry company (Hangzhou Nuowei).

findings: FedSDA addresses stain/scanner shift between centers in federated tumour classification. Each client decomposes its H&E patches into a stain matrix and density map (Vahadane stain separation); a small diffusion model trained by FedAvg on the stain matrices only (not the images) lets each client resample other clients' stains, so every client's images are re-rendered with a mix of all clients' stains before an ordinary federated classifier is trained. It lifted tumour AUROC for five federated baselines, most strongly on the six-scanner prostate set, and beat two other data-side alignment methods (CCST, amplitude normalisation). It is label-free and needs no test-time processing, unlike normalisation-layer methods. The privacy argument (stain matrices are lower risk than images) is asserted by citation to attacks on federated diffusion models; no attack or defence is run on FedSDA.
numbers: Clients (each scanner or centre is one client): MA14 2 scanners, 35,996 and 35,993 patches; CAMELYON17 5 centres, 10 WSIs each, 34,832 to 146,721 patches; AGGC22 6 scanners, 22-38 WSIs each, 115,163 to 254,366 patches. Rounds: diffusion model 3 rounds x 300 local epochs (single-layer transformer, 13.2K parameters, FD 0.40; MLP version 4.7K parameters FD 18.91); classifier DenseNet-121, 100 rounds, 1 local epoch. caveats: Reports federated vs federated baselines only: there is no pooled (centralized) or local-only arm, so the gap to pooled training is not measurable from this paper. Privacy claim is by argument; no leakage test of the stain-matrix diffusion model or differential privacy cost is given. findings: For fixed-effects meta-analysis with maximum-likelihood summary statistics, the inverse-information-weighted combination of per-study estimates has the same asymptotic distribution as the maximum likelihood estimate from pooled individual-level data, for parametric and semiparametric models including linear, logistic and Cox regression. The equivalence needs a shared effect and study-specific nuisance parameters; it is exact numerically only in special cases (equal-variance linear model, score test statistic). With a common nuisance parameter such as a shared intercept, univariate summaries lose efficiency unless the per-study covariance between effect and nuisance estimators scales identically (zero covariance suffices); sending the joint multivariate estimate and information matrix restores it. Random-effects models are left to a separate report. This is the theoretical basis for one-round, summary-statistic fits of a prediction head.
numbers: Estimator: beta_hat = (sum_k I_k)^-1 sum_k I_k beta_hat_k with variance (sum_k I_k)^-1 (Eqs 3-4); pooled MLE has the same form with I_k evaluated at the pooled estimate (Eq 5). Simulation Table 1 (K=2, logistic, 1 million replicates per row), beta1=beta2=0.8, n=100+100: SE 0.302 (summary) vs 0.304 (individual), power 0.772 vs 0.775. With unequal effects (beta1 not equal to beta2) the two methods differ more; original-data meta-analysis was usually a little more powerful, for example power 0.665 (summary) vs 0.685 (individual) in one K=2 row and 0.500 vs 0.553 in the row with the largest effect gap (Table 1, exact beta values not re-checked per row). Table 2 relative efficiency (K = 20, 50, 100; n = 10 to 100): summary with common intercept vs individual with common intercept RE1 1.047-1.161; summary with separate intercepts vs individual with common intercept RE2 0.966-1.022; separate vs separate RE3 1.030-1.113. Major-depression GWAS example: 3 replication samples (1,907, 2,489, 2,005 subjects; 3,135 cases, 3,266 controls), 30 SNPs; largest absolute difference in log odds ratio 0.00066 and largest relative difference in SE 0.25% when sex effects are study-specific; 0.0045 and 0.35% when pooled with a common sex effect.
locations: Summary; Section 1; Section 2.1 (main result, Eqs 1-5); 2.2 (common nuisance parameters, Lemma 1); 2.3 (unequal effect sizes, score statistics identical); 2.4 (linear, logistic, Cox examples); Section 3.1 Tables 1-2; Section 3.2; Section 4 Remarks; Appendices A-B
caveats: Fixed-effects (common beta) setting; asymptotics are in per-study size n_k with finite K. The paper does not treat random-effects models, high-dimensional parameters or penalised estimators, so extension to a ridge or many-gene head with covariate shift is not covered here. Equivalence is asymptotic, not an identity, for estimators with study-specific variance estimates; a ridge head solved from pooled sufficient statistics (X'X, X'y) is a different, exact construction not in this paper. Small or sparse studies can make per-study estimates undefined; the authors note pooling is more stable then. The 'unequal effect' power results come from simulation only, with K=2.

findings: FedBN keeps batch-normalisation layers (scale, shift and running statistics) local to each client and averages everything else with FedAvg, which handles feature-shift non-IID data (different scanners or protocols with the same labels). It adds no tuning parameters and no extra communication, and the authors give a convergence argument for a two-layer over-parameterised network under feature shift. On digits, Office-Caltech10, DomainNet and the ABIDE neuroimaging sites it beats FedAvg, FedProx and local-only training, with the largest gains for the most shifted client and for clients with small local data. Relevance to the review: a cheap personalisation route for a CNN or transformer-with-BN head or encoder when centers differ in stain, scanner or platform.
numbers: Benchmark: 5 digit datasets (SVHN, USPS, SynthDigits, MNIST-M, MNIST), 5 clients, 7,438 training samples each (10% default size per client); local epochs E tested 1, 4, 8, 16, accuracy falls as E rises for both methods. Heterogeneity sweep up to 10 clients per domain. Table 1 mean accuracy (5 trials), SingleSet / FedAvg / FedProx / FedBN: Office-Caltech10 Amazon 54.9/54.1/54.2/63.0, Caltech 40.2/44.8/44.5/45.3, DSLR 78.7/66.9/65.0/83.1, Webcam 86.4/85.1/84.4/90.5; DomainNet Clipart 41.0/48.8/48.9/51.2, Infograph 23.8/24.9/24.9/26.8, Painting 36.2/36.5/36.6/41.5, Quickdraw 73.1/56.1/54.4/71.3, Real 48.5/46.3/47.8/54.8, Sketch 34.0/36.6/36.9/42.1; ABIDE (4 sites) NYU 58.0/62.7/63.3/65.6, USM 73.4/73.1/73.0/75.1, UM 64.3/70.7/70.5/68.6, UCLA 57.3/64.7/64.5/65.5. caveats: Classification only; no regression or expression targets, and no pooled-training arm is reported (baselines are SingleSet, FedAvg, FedProx). Convergence proof is for a two-layer ReLU network with a shared covariance structure per client and gradient descent, not deep nets. Clients are small (about 100 to 1,000 samples). A client whose BN statistics are never seen by the federation needs access to averaged BN parameters at test time (Appendix G). The authors list the privacy effect of hidden BN parameters as untested. Gains do not hold at every site (ABIDE UM).

findings: Using 384 breast cancer slides each scanned on five scanners, the study isolates scanner effects from lab and biology. Frozen embeddings from 14 encoders (13 pathology foundation models plus ImageNet ResNet) cluster by scanner for most vision-only transformers, and neighbour rankings between scanners are distorted. Slide-level attention-MIL heads trained on TCGA-BRCA and tested on the multi-scanner set keep similar AUC across scanners, but class decisions agree less across scanners and predicted probabilities shift systematically (calibration bias). Robustness did not track model size, recency or training set size: newer or larger models (UNI2-h, Virchow2, H-Optimus-1) were not more robust than their predecessors, and vision-language CONCH and CONCHv1.5 and the distilled H0-mini were the most stable but not the most accurate. Direct bearing on Q4: a frozen-encoder federation inherits scanner offsets that the encoder does not remove, and the effect appears as a shift in score level rather than rank.
numbers: CHIME Multiscanner: 384 patients, one hospital (Sodersjukhuset), five scanners from three makers (G20X, G40X, PHIL, HXR1, HXR2), 1,920 WSIs. Training cohort TCGA-BRCA 825 primary tumours from more than 40 tissue source sites; ten stratified 80/20 splits; 10 x 5 = 50 evaluations per encoder and task. Five tasks: ER, PR, HER2, binary NHG 1v3, three-class NHG. 1-NN cross-scanner match rate for G20X-PHIL: CONCHv1.5 81.8%, Phikon-v2 25.8%. Fleiss kappa across the five scanners ranges about 0.4 (Phikon-v2, HER2) to 0.85 (CONCHv1.5, ER). HER2 positive 8.8% in CHIME. Encoders trained on from about 20K to 3.1 million slides; embedding dimension 512-2,560. AUC: all ViT-based encoders similar within bootstrap CIs (1,000 resamples); UNI and H-Optimus top; RetCCL and ResNet-IN lower; G20X lowest AUC on NHG for most encoders (exact AUC values are in Fig. 7 bars, not tabulated in the text).
locations: Abstract; Section 3.1 (datasets, Table 1), 3.3 (encoders, Table 2); Section 4.1.2 (five embedding metrics), 4.2 (ABMIL, Fleiss kappa, LOWESS calibration); Section 5.1 Figs 4-6; Section 5.2 Figs 7-10; Section 6 Discussion and 6.3 Limitations; Supplement Figs S1-S5
caveats: Breast cancer slides and a single tissue; scanner shift only, with no stain-lab or platform shift and no federation or mitigation tested. Not a gene-expression prediction study; tasks are clinicopathological labels with an attention-MIL head. Slide embeddings are mean-pooled tile features; tiles are not registered across scanners. Quantitative per-encoder AUC and kappa values are in figures only, so I give ranges. CHIME is not public. The conclusion that robustness is not a function of scale is across 14 models that differ in architecture and data, not a controlled scaling experiment (the authors say they cannot separate multimodal alignment from data diversity).

findings: A 10x Genomics study on serial FFPE sections of two breast tumours using single-cell Flex (scFFPE-seq), Visium CytAssist and Xenium, with H&E on the same sections. It is a platform comparison, not a prediction or federation paper: Visium and Flex share one 18,536-gene probe set, whereas Xenium used a 313-gene targeted panel (280 plus 33 add-on), so the three platforms measure different gene sets at different resolution and sensitivity, and integration needed registration of images, cell-type transfer and spot interpolation. Relevance to Q4: this quantifies how far platform differences move the data a center would hold, and shows why a federation across Visium, Visium HD and Xenium sites must handle partial gene overlap and different counts per unit area.
numbers: Visium and Flex: 18,536 genes targeted by 54,018 probes; Visium median 5,712 genes per spot; scFFPE-seq median 1,480 genes per cell, 17 clusters in both. Xenium: 313 genes (1.8% of transcriptome), 167,885 cells, 36,944,521 transcripts, median 166 transcripts per cell, median 62 genes per cell vs 34 for scFFPE-seq downsampled to the same 313 genes; 86% of cells assigned a single supervised type. Over the common capture area (78% of Visium), Visium had 3.6x more total transcripts; Xenium median gene sensitivity was 8.4x Visium on the panel genes; TACSTD2 Visium vs Xenium counts r2 = 0.88; serial-section replicate transcript counts r2 = 0.99. A triple-positive ERBB2/ESR1/PGR region covered about 5-6 Visium spots; 48 and 44 differentially expressed genes (log2FC > 1.5, p < 0.05) against the two PGR-negative DCIS regions.

caveats: Two tumours from two patients, one block per tumour for single-cell data (N = 1 for scFFPE-seq); no outcome prediction, no learning curves, no federation. The sensitivity ratios (8.4x, 3.6x) are specific to this panel, tissue and assay generation, and come from supplementary figures that I did not open; the main text states them. Authors are 10x Genomics employees. Xenium gene panel was chosen from breast atlas data, so panel composition is itself a design choice that differs by center. Visium HD is not covered.

findings: A malicious analyst with ordinary access to a federated analysis can recover a data owner's individual-level values from nothing more than repeated mean and covariance queries: the analyst sends n_j known linearly independent vectors to a site holding n_j records, asks for each covariance with the attacked variable, and solves a linear system. The reconstruction is exact to numerical precision on a DataSHIELD test set, works in TensorFlow Federated, and is feasible in PyTorch-based platforms; zero-mean noise on the returned statistics is averaged away by repeating the attack. Differential privacy blocks the attack only when the budget is so tight that a single ordinary covariance exhausts it. This bears on Q5 for any route that releases summary statistics, because the leak is a property of the query interface, not of the statistic.
numbers: CNSIM test data: 3 servers, 9,379 synthetic observations, 11 variables; attacked server 1 with complete cases n_j = 250 for BMI: Pearson correlation between true and reconstructed values 1.0, maximum absolute error 2e-12. Attack needs n_j queries; matrix solve scales O(n_j^3) but contributed 7e-6 percent of wall time at the largest size, so communication dominates. Noise defence: repeated runs R up to 1,000, 200 replicates; reconstruction error shrinks with R. DataSHIELD guards: n_j > 3 for mean and n_j > 6 for covariance, each level of a binary variable at least 3 times. Differential privacy: epsilon varied between ln(1.01) and ln(3); within that budget the attacker could not run enough repetitions to average out noise, but one covariance among the five metric CNSIM variables already used the whole budget, so a standard mean-variance-covariance workflow could not be completed. DataSHIELD 6.4 will block the relevant functions by default after the authors informed the developers.
locations: Abstract; Section 2.1 (Algorithm 1, Eqs 1-2, tools T1-T3); 2.2 (complexity, Fig 3); 2.3.1-2.3.4 (DataSHIELD, noise robustness Fig 4, TensorFlow Federated, PyTorch platforms); 2.3.5 (differential privacy, Fig 5); Section 3 Discussion
caveats: Threat model: an attacker with client credentials who can send arbitrary vectors to the site and receive covariances; a fixed, pre-agreed release of sufficient statistics (for example one X'X and X'y per site) without such queries is not the attacked interface, though that conclusion is my reading, not a claim in the paper. Tested on tabular clinical variables, not on image embeddings or expression profiles, and on synthetic CNSIM data. Linear case only; the authors say nonlinear risks persist. The paper does not report how many records a site must hold for the attack to become infeasible beyond the n_j-query cost. Privacy accounting is simple composition.

findings: PPML-Omics adds Gaussian differential privacy and a random exchange of gradients between hospitals (decentralised randomisation) to federated training, tested on TCGA bulk RNA-seq (37 cancers), scRNA-seq clustering, and H&E to spatial expression with ST-Net. Plain federation protects little (attack JS divergence stays near the centralized value), while differential privacy blocks the reconstruction attacks at the price of accuracy that grows as the budget tightens. In the spatial task the published table does separate the arms: federated alone is slightly worse than centralized, DP-federated explodes at small epsilon, and PPML-Omics sits in between. The preprint's near-identical MSE for every arm (about 0.91) is not what the published table shows, so the published version should be cited. Note that the paper is an assignment outside my seven listed papers; I read it because the instructions asked for it.
